chunk_findings.detail: `update_message` builds its output from an arbitrary dict, and it treats the two "dropped" keys inconsistently: the needs branch guards with `data.get("needs_dropped")` (correctly allowing the key to be absent, since it is only produced on a replacing update), but the globs branch is gated on `"globs" in data["fields"]` and then hard-indexes `data["globs_dropped"]`. So the function's own contract — demonstrated by the sibling check — permits a payload that carries `fields["globs"]` without a `globs_dropped` entry, and such a payload raises `KeyError: 'globs_dropped'` instead of printing the message. Concretely, the non-replacing glob paths (`--add-globs` / `--remove-globs`, which change the list without dropping anything, and which the sibling `flag_exempt` entries show are live flags) put `globs` into `fields`; if any such path does not also populate `globs_dropped`, `ddflow update <id> --add-globs X` now dies while formatting its result message rather than reporting the update. The fix is to gate (or read) `globs_dropped` the same way the needs branch does, e.g. `if data.get("globs_dropped"):` / `data.get("globs_dropped", [])`.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent for this bug says the fix is `--add-needs` / `--remove-needs` "and the same for `--globs` and `--tags`", because `--tags`, like `--needs`, silently replaces the whole list. The updated golden help output for `ddflow update -h` — which is the authoritative enumeration of the command's options in this change — shows `--add-globs` / `--remove-globs` (pre-existing, as the intent notes for globs) but no `--add-tags` / `--remove-tags`, and the diff adds no test asserting that `--tags` reports what it dropped either. So the replace-only bug class is fixed only for `--needs`: `ddflow update ID --tags X` still discards the item's existing tags with no way to add or remove a single tag and (per the tests added here) no assertion that it prints the dropped values the way `--globs`/`--needs` now do. Anyone reorganising tags across many items still needs the read-modify-write workaround the change was meant to eliminate. Either add the tag options (and their help/snapshot entries) or make `--tags` print the dropped values, and cover it with a test analogous to the ones added here.

chunk_findings.detail: `or` short-circuits, so whenever `_adjust_needs` produces its "nothing to change" message (it returns a non-empty string exactly when `fields["needs"] == list(it.needs) and len(fields) == 1`), `_adjust_globs` is never called and the glob edit is silently dropped. Because `_adjust_needs` runs *before* the globs adjuster folds anything into `fields`, the `len(fields) == 1` guard is still true when only `--add-needs`/`--remove-needs` and `--add-globs`/`--remove-globs` are given, so this is the common case, not a corner one. Concrete input: `ddflow update ID --add-needs A --add-globs new/path/**` where `A` is already in `it.needs` and no other field flag is passed. `_adjust_needs` sets `fields["needs"]` to the unchanged list, `len(fields) == 1`, returns the reason, the `or` never evaluates `_adjust_globs`, and the command returns `O.nothing(...)` — the new glob is not written and the user is told "nothing to change", even though the glob list would have changed. The two folds must both run (e.g. `unchanged = _adjust_needs(...); unchanged = _adjust_globs(...) or unchanged`) for the combined-flag edit to be correct.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent is `--add-needs` / `--remove-needs` "and the same for `--globs` and `--tags`", because `--tags`, like `--needs`, replaces the whole list and reports nothing about what it dropped. The change adds `add_needs`/`remove_needs` to `ddflow/api/items.py` and wires `--add-needs`/`--remove-needs` in `ddflow/surfaces/cli.py`, but the command surface (and the help snapshot, which is the authoritative enumeration of the options after this change) still has no `--add-tags` / `--remove-tags` and no `tags_dropped` reporting. chunk_findings.detail:
The generalized adjuster inherits the `or` short-circuit of the function it replaced, and the newly-added tags path is now a victim of it. `_adjust_list` returns a non-empty string exactly when the list it just folded equals the item's current list *and* `len(fields) == 1`. Because `--add-needs`/`--remove-needs` is evaluated first, an edit that is only a no-op needs change plus a real tag change leaves `fields` holding just `{"needs": ...}`, so `_adjust_list(..., "needs")` returns its "nothing to change" message, `or` short-circuits, and `_adjust_list(..., "tags")` is never called. The tags edit is neither applied nor reported.

Concrete input: item `ID` has `needs = ["a"]` and `tags = ["t1"]`; run `ddflow update ID --remove-needs b --add-tags t2`. The needs fold produces `["a"]` (equal to current), `fields` has length 1, so `_adjust_list` returns `"nothing to change: --add-needs ... --remove-needs name none of a."`, `_adjust_list(..., "tags")` is skipped, `fields["tags"]` is never set, and the call returns `O.nothing(...)` — `t2` is silently dropped and `tags_dropped` reports nothing. This is a new defect of the new code (the tags surface is new), and it demonstrates the rewrite did not answer the earlier short-circuit finding: the first adjuster can still swallow every later one (tags here, and globs as before) whenever the earlier fold is a no-op.

chunk_findings.detail: The new parameter is declared `cli_only=True`, and the justification string in `flag_exempt` states the intended behaviour over MCP: `"CLI only: over MCP \`ddflow_update\` sets them (tools/list byte budget)"`. That means the MCP entry point for creating a task, the tool `ddflow_task_add` that this same declared command defines, still cannot carry resources. Concrete scenario: an agent (which typically drives ddflow through the MCP tools, not the shell) calls `ddflow_task_add` with the equivalent of `gpu:4`; the call is accepted, `task_add` is invoked with the default `resources=""`, `_csv_or_none("")` yields `None`, and the task is persisted with no resource recorded — exactly the state the bug report says is claimable ("a GPU task … is claimable without its resource declared in between"). The agent then has to issue a separate `ddflow_update` call, recreating the same window the fix was meant to close. So the reported failure mode is only fixed on the CLI surface; on the MCP surface the two-step, race-prone workflow is preserved (and made harder to notice, because the tool schema advertises no way to declare resources at add time). Note also the inconsistency this creates inside the file: the declared handler still does `resources=a.get("resources", "")` for this tool, i.e. it will happily honour the key if a client sends it, while the schema/`flag_exempt` declares the key unavailable over MCP — so the capability is hidden from discovery rather than actually absent. A complete fix would either expose `resources` on `ddflow_task_add` (the byte-budget justification is a tooling constraint, not a correctness reason) or make the claim path refuse a task whose resources were never set.

chunk_findings.detail: The task branch of `_candidates` no longer filters by `i.kind == "task"` but by `i.is_work`. `is_work` is the broad "every kind but a phase is task-like" predicate — the same change's own comment in `workflow.py` states "every kind but a phase is task-like" — so `_candidates(st, "task", cfg)` now returns *every* non-phase item, not just tasks. Concretely, in a state that holds one task and one bug (kind `"bug"`), `_candidates(st, "task", cfg)` returns the bug item as well, so `ddflow task list` reports the bug as a task, and any task-scoped resolution/action (e.g. `ddflow task show <bug-id>`, `ddflow complete <bug-id>` through the task path) now accepts the bug and applies the task pipeline's gates to it instead of the bug kind's. The same item is also returned by `_candidates(st, "bug", cfg)`, so it is served under two viewers simultaneously. If the intent was only to make the newly-supported doc/research/job kinds visible to the task viewer, the predicate should have named exactly those kinds (`i.kind in ("task", "doc", "research", "job")`), not the catch-all `is_work`; with `is_work` the change silently widens an existing viewer's scope to kinds it was never meant to handle.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent is that `task add --kind doc` *(and research/job)* is wired to `kind_pipelines`, and the bug premise is that "a document, a research item or a scheduled job gets its own gates" and that a research item (the `docs/RESEARCH.md` / DDFLOWUP021.1 entry) had to run the code-task pipeline and was refused. In this updated fixture only `kind_pipelines.doc` was reduced to `["rules","implement","standards","dedupe","merge"]`; `kind_pipelines.research` and `kind_pipelines.job` are byte-for-byte the full task pipeline (`research, rules, implement, rubber_duck, critic, standards, unit_tests, bug_hunt, dedupe, merge`), and `unit_tests` is still listed in `rules."gates.required"` (`["implement","unit_tests","merge"]`). So for input `ddflow task add --kind research --title ...` (or `--kind job`) followed by completion, the selected pipeline still contains the required `unit_tests` gate and `ddflow complete` still refuses with `required gate(s) not passed: unit_tests` – exactly the failure the change claims to fix. Only the doc kind is unblocked; the research/job kinds the intent names remain broken.

chunk_findings.detail: The stimulus for the "incoherent workflow edit is REFUSED" assertion was changed from a real gate (`"gates": "unit_tests"`) to a string that is not a gate name at all (`"gates": "tasks"`). Before this hunk the refusal was produced by the coherence rule the comment describes: setting `which: "task"` to the single gate `unit_tests` drops the task kind's mandatory `implement` gate, so the edit is rejected. After the change the request is rejected (if it is rejected) only because `tasks` matches no known gate; the coherence check for a task pipeline is no longer exercised by this test at all. Concretely: if the `kind_pipelines` rework in parts 1–14 relaxed or re-routed the validation such that `ddflow_workflow_pipeline --which task --gates unit_tests --dry-run` now returns success, this test stays green while the tool would actually rewrite the task pipeline to `[unit_tests]` — a task kind whose `ddflow complete` never requires `implement`, which is precisely the "pipeline gates do not match the item's kind" failure this change set out to fix. The edit silently trades a real incoherence case for a nonexistent-name case; the refusal path exercised is no longer the one named by the test's comment.

chunk_findings.detail: `readme_with_code` is the code↔docs coupling rule ("an item that changed code must also have updated docs"). Its implementation never checks whether the item changed code: it only checks the item's kind and then looks up a gate literally named `"docs"`. Previously it was scoped to `kind == "task"`, i.e. to the code pipeline whose gates include `docs`. The change to `not it.is_work` now runs it for every work kind, including `doc`. A doc item created with `ddflow task add --kind doc` runs the shiped doc pipeline (which drops `unit_tests` and, by the same reasoning, does not carry a gate named `docs`), so `it.gates.get("docs")` is falsy and the function returns its non-empty "readme not satisfied" reason. With `[enforce] readme_with_code` set to anything other than `off`, `ddflow complete` on that doc item is then refused for a condition the doc pipeline can never satisfy — the same "docs forced through a rule built for code tasks" failure the change is meant to remove (the only exits remain `--force` or an open lease). The filter should stay task-scoped, or skip items that changed no code/globs.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion's own comment states the contract being tested: "an edit that would leave the workflow incoherent is REFUSED, before writing." The previous input, `which: "task", gates: "unit_tests"`, exercised exactly that: a *known* gate set that drops the mandatory gates for the code-task pipeline (`implement`, `review`), i.e. a semantically incoherent pipeline that must be rejected (this is the same required-gate enforcement that `ddflow complete` reports as "required gate(s) not passed: implement, unit_tests"). The replacement input, `gates: "tasks"`, is not a gate name at all, so the call now takes the unknown-gate/unknown-pipeline error path. The test still passes (`isError is True`) but no longer covers the incoherence validation it claims to cover, and it passes for an unrelated reason. The only situation in which this substitution is necessary is that `gates: "unit_tests"` has stopped being refused for `which: "task"` — i.e. the mandatory `implement`/`review` gates for kind `task` are no longer enforced, in which case a code task could be re-authored with only `unit_tests` and completed with gates skipped, which is precisely the failure mode this change set claims to close for other kinds. chunk_findings.detail: The change makes the fold kind-aware only on the *creation* path: `"task.added"` now passes `work_kind(ev.data)` to `_h_added`, so `task add --kind doc` really produces an `Item(kind="doc")`. But the two sibling handlers that mutate an existing item were left hardcoded to the literal `"task"`: `"task.updated": lambda st, ev: _h_updated(st, ev, "task")` and (just below) `"task.removed": ...  _h_removed(st, ev, "task")`. Those functions receive `kind` for exactly one reason — to match the target item — the same reason `_h_added` receives it to stamp the new item's kind; `st.items` is a flat `id -> Item` map and each `Item` already carries its own `kind`, so the parameter can only be a kind check. Concretely: after `task add --kind doc` folds item `d1` with `kind="doc"`, any later `task update d1 ...` emits a `task.updated` event with `id=d1`, the handler calls `_h_updated(st, ev, "task")`, and the guard `i.kind != kind` (`"doc" != "task"`) drops the update (or raises, depending on the guard): the doc item's title/needs/tags can never change. Removal is symmetrically broken, so a doc/research/job item created by this feature is effectively immutable. The fix used for `.added` (`work_kind(ev.data)`) must be applied to the `.updated`/`.removed` handlers too (or they must stop matching on the literal kind).

chunk_findings.detail: `--kind` is accepted as an arbitrary, unvalidated string. The Param declares no `choices` and the value is threaded straight through (`kind=getattr(a, "kind", None) or ""` in `commands/queue.py`, `kind=a.get("kind", "") or ""` in the declared surface) with no normalization or rejection, even though the help text advertises exactly `task`, `doc`, `research` or `job`. So `ddflow task add --title X --kind Doc` (or `--kind docs`, `--kind bug`, `--kind docc`) succeeds and stores an item whose kind is not in `WORK_KINDS`. Two consequences follow directly from this same diff: (1) because the change rewired `_candidates(st, "task", …)` in `ddflow/services/viewers.py:171` to filter by `i.is_work` instead of `i.kind == "task"`, such an item no longer shows up in `ddflow task list` at all; and (2) `workflow.py` only registers pipelines for `task`, `phase`, `doc` and explicit `kind_pipelines` entries, so no pipeline is configured for the typo'd kind — its required-gate set falls back to either the empty set (so `ddflow complete` passes with no gates enforced) or the code-task pipeline (so it is refused for `unit_tests`, exactly the bug this change was meant to remove). Either way the user gets a hidden item that cannot be worked normally. This needs `choices=("task","doc","research","job")` on the Param, or a validation/normalization step in the add handler.

chunk_findings.detail: The test is meant to prove that `readme_with_code` "stays a task rule" — i.e. that a doc-kind item is exempt — but it never creates the condition the rule keys on, so it cannot distinguish a doc from a task. `_doc(repo)` creates the item with `--globs docs/x.md` and the test never claims or modifies it, so the item has no code change at all. `readme_with_code` "couples CODE changes to the README", so with zero code changes `readme_report(st, cfg, "D1", repo=repo)` returns `""` for *any* kind. Concretely: if the fix were absent/vacuous and `readme_with_code="block"` were still enforced on doc-kind items, this assertion would still see `""` and pass, because there is no code path in `docs/x.md` and no working-tree change to inspect. To actually exercise the exemption the item would need to touch code (e.g. `--globs "a.py"`) and/or have a recorded code change, so that the unfixed behaviour yields the block message and the fixed behaviour yields `""`; as written the test gives false confidence for the kind exemption it names. This weakens the mandatory regression coverage for the fix (see [D-rules-hierarchy]).

chunk_findings.detail: The test is meant to prove that `readme_with_code` "stays a task rule" — i.e. that a doc-kind item is exempt — but it never creates the condition the rule keys on, so it cannot distinguish a doc from a task. `_doc(repo)` creates the item with `--globs docs/x.md` and the test never claims or modifies it, so the item has no code change at all. `readme_with_code` "couples CODE changes to the README", so with zero code changes `readme_report(st, cfg, "D1", repo=repo)` returns `""` for *any* kind. Concretely: if the fix were absent/vacuous and `readme_with_code="block"` were still enforced on doc-kind items, this assertion would still see `""` and pass, because there is no code path in `docs/x.md` and no working-tree change to inspect. To actually exercise the exemption the item would need to touch code (e.g. `--globs "a.py"`) and/or have a recorded code change, so that the unfixed behaviour yields the block message and the fixed behaviour yields `""`; as written the test gives false confidence for the kind exemption it names. This weakens the mandatory regression coverage for the fix (see [D-rules-hierarchy]).
